big: Two funds follow the same Nifty 50 index. On the same day they still show slightly different returns. This is not a mistake. Two small numbers explain it, and they tell you which fund to choose.

lines: Both funds track the Nifty 50. Why do their returns differ?
Because following an index is never perfect. Two measures capture the imperfection, and they are not the same thing.

h: Same index, a small gap that grows
alt: Three lines for an index and two index funds following it, with the funds slightly below the index at the end
caps: A made-up index and two funds that follow it. The paths look almost the same.
Fund A costs 0.2% a year, and Fund B costs 0.7%. Each lags the index by about its cost.
Look at the end boxes. After ten years the gap is visible, even though the lines were hard to tell apart.
That gap in return over a period is tracking difference. It is mostly the expense ratio.

rows: Average gap to index (basis points a year)
Day to day wiggle of the gap (basis points)
alt: Bars comparing two funds with the same average gap to the index but a different day to day wiggle
caps: Now two funds with the same cost. Both trail the index by about 20 basis points a year.
Fund A's daily gap stays steady, within about 3 basis points. Its tracking error is low.
Fund C's gap swings about 25 basis points a day, from cash drag and late rebalancing. Assumed figures.
Tracking difference is how far behind. Tracking error is how jumpy the gap is. Lower is better for both.

h: What a small gap does over time
small: Fund A over Fund B, after 20 years
alt: Bars showing how much more a cheaper index fund leaves on a ten lakh rupee investment
caps: Take ₹10 lakh and an index returning 12%. Fund A keeps 11.8% a year. Fund B keeps 11.3%.
The gap in rupees starts small. After 2 years it is about ₹0.1 lakh.
It grows every year, because the gap earns returns as well.
After 20 years the cheaper fund leaves about ₹8.0 lakh more. Small gaps compound.

q: Over three years the Nifty 50 index gave 40.0%. Meena's two index funds gave 39.4% and 38.1%. Which statement is correct?
opts: The second fund has the lower tracking error, as it earned less
Both lag by the same amount, since the index is the same
The first fund lags by about 0.6 points, the second 1.9
The first fund beat the index, since 39.4% is close to 40%
why: A lower return does not mean a lower tracking error. Tracking error is about how jumpy the daily gap is.
Their returns differ, so their gaps differ. The same index does not mean the same tracking difference.
Tracking difference is the gap to the index: 40.0 minus 39.4 is 0.6, and 40.0 minus 38.1 is 1.9.
Neither fund beat the index. Both gave less than 40%, and an index fund is expected to lag a little.

q: Fund X has the lowest expense ratio of all Nifty 50 funds. Yet its daily returns often differ from the index by a visible margin. What does this show?
opts: Low cost does not ensure tight tracking, so check error too
A cheap fund must have a low tracking error by definition
The index must be wrong, since the fund is cheap and follows it
Tracking error matters only for ETFs, not for index funds
why: A fund can charge little and still run loosely, with cash drag or late rebalancing. Both numbers are worth a look.
Cost and tracking are separate. A cheap fund managed carelessly can still show a jumpy gap to its index.
The index is a fixed list with fixed weights. The gap comes from how the fund copies it, not from the index.
Tracking error applies to every fund that copies an index, whether sold as an index fund or an ETF.

q: Meena's index fund charges 0.20% a year but trailed its index by 0.45% last year. Where might the other 0.25% come from?
opts: A hidden charge the fund house adds on top of the expense ratio
Cash drag, rebalancing delays and the timing of dividends
The manager's wrong calls about which shares to hold in it
SEBI deducts the difference from every index fund each year
why: The expense ratio is disclosed and capped by rules. The extra gap comes from how the fund copies the index.
Small frictions add to the gap: cash waiting to be invested, delays after index changes, and dividend timing.
An index fund does not choose shares, so no calls were made. It follows the index list.
No regulator deducts from index funds. Normal frictions in copying explain the gap.

q: Two funds follow the same index. Fund P has expense 0.30% and tracking difference 0.35%. Fund Q has expense 0.15% and tracking difference 0.40%. Which would an informed adviser prefer?
opts: Fund Q, since its expense ratio is lower and that is what counts
Either, since 0.05% a year is too small to bother with
Neither, since an index fund always lags by its expense ratio
Fund P, whose tracking difference is lower, so it leaves more
why: Expense ratio is one part of the gap. Q's actual gap is larger, so its lower fee was not enough.
0.05% a year compounds over decades. It is small each year and still real, so it is a fair tiebreaker.
The gap is mostly the expense ratio, plus friction. Funds differ, so comparing them is useful.
The investor earns index minus tracking difference. P trails by 0.35% and Q by 0.40%, so P leaves more.

pts: Tracking difference is the gap in return from the index. It is mostly the expense ratio.
Tracking error is how jumpy that gap is. Lower is better for both.
Compare funds on the same index by tracking difference over one to three years.
